messages.subject: Abundance models for the spread of invasions
messages.subject_clean: Abundance models for the spread of invasions
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
                    I have a quick question and I thought this will be an excellent forum to find some leads. I’m looking at the spread of invasive big headed ants in a pretty homogeneous savanna in Kenya. I have several transects perpendicular to the invasion front and at each transect I have baiting stations from well behind the front towards the front of the invasion. I have counts within seasons (baiting is separated 1-2 days and although they reproduce continuously is fair to assume N does not vary) and between seasons to monitor the spread. Ideally I would like to model the spread of big headed ants  using a state space model that includes some sort of population growth function and diffusion.

An alternative would be to model just population growth rate  and then estimate diffusion using the speeds of invasion I observed in the field.

Any insights on this will be very much appreciated,

Thanks

Alejandro

messages.subject: Different values in BUGSoutput$summary and BUGSoutput$mean
messages.subject_clean: Different values in BUGSoutput$summary and BUGSoutput$mean
messages.body_plain:
I ran a state-space model in R using R2jags package and I noticed a strange issue in the model output. Among parameters calculated by the model I have a deterministic node, that is, log counts backtransformed.

Nh[g,t] <- exp(logNh[g,t])

where g and t are respectively site and time indices

In the model output (out <- jags(...))the means reported on out$BUGSoutput$mean and out$BUGSoutput$summary do no correspond from a certain time point on

cbind(out$BUGSoutput$mean$Nh[1,][fc[g]:lc[g]], out$BUGSoutput$summary["Nh[1,fc[g]:lc[g]",1])
#fc and lc represents first and last count circumstances, different among sites

              [,1]     [,2]
Nh[1,1]   7.889378 7.889378
Nh[1,2]   7.461558 7.461558
Nh[1,3]   7.212565 7.212565
Nh.....   ........ ........
Nh[1,9]   5.180559 5.180559
Nh[1,10]  4.987814 4.987814
Nh[1,11]  5.780468 4.689696 #here it starts diverging
Nh[1,12]  1.181960 4.311867
Nh[1,13]  2.050339 3.920243
Nh[1,14] 25.607913 3.693816
Nh[1,15]  4.915882 3.549902

I tried to calculate manually the means accessing the MCMC chains (iterations=100000, burning=50000, thinnning=9, 3 chains), to test which output is the correct. For example, the mean of the node Nh[1,14] resulted

Nh <- aperm(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$Nh, c(2,3,1)) # simple array transposition to stack iterations
mean(Nh[1,14,])

 [1] 25.60791

I cannot understand this difference in the reported means.

Of course, this happens to all other parameters.

This issue happens only when I limit parameter estimation to a last circumstance (the "lc"), otherwise it works fine (but the model is somehow wrong, since it calculates parameters for time points in whichI have no data...). There may be something wrong in the model I wrote, but even so, how could the values be different?

Is that something wrong related to the function that calculates the ....$summary?

It must be noted that the results of the ....$summary are more "reasonable", since they correspond to the results I get when I do no limit the parameter estimation to the first/last circumstance.

Thank you,

Alessio

messages.subject: Re: Different values in BUGSoutput$summary and BUGSoutput$mean
messages.subject_clean: Different values in BUGSoutput$summary and BUGSoutput$mean
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alessio,

I haven't used R2jags for a long time (prefer jagsUI), but here's my 2c worth:

Looking at the source code, R2jags calls R2WinBUGS::monitor to get the summary values. These are then chopped up and reordered to produce the $mean and $summary output. The most likely reason that your 2 columns are different is that the values are in different orders. Check the means of the 2 columns: if identical, then ordering is the problem. Check the row names for $mean and $summary, and if incorrect inform the package maintainer (and good luck with that!).

BTW not sure why you used aperm, mean(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$Nh[, 1, 14]) should work fine and be slightly more efficient. You can get the whole matrix of means with apply(out$BUGSoutput$sims.list$Nh, 2:3, mean).

Regards, Mike

messages.subject: AHMbook R package is now on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: AHMbook R package is now on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
The AHMbook package is now available from CRAN and can be installed with install.packages("AHMbook") and updated with update.packages("AHMbook"). Or you can use the menus, but with >10,000 packages to choose from, it's quicker to type.
The packages on which AHMbook depends will automatically be downloaded and installed.

This is a new version, v.0.1.3, with the following changes:
Function pcount.spHDS and predict methods for unmarkedFit objects have moved to the unmarked package v.0.12 (thanks to Andy Royle); AHMbook now Depends on the new version (0.12) of unmarked.
Added the MHB2014, SwissSquirrels, SwissTits, Finnmark, ttdPeregrine and wagtail data sets; see the help files for ways to use these instead of .csv files with the code in the book.
Removed default arguments for the coordinates in map.Nmix.resi, making it more generally useful (and acceptable on CRAN).
Fixed: slew of warnings produced by simNmix, also dropping of dimensions with small numbers of individuals.
Added more examples to the help pages for simulation functions.

If you find that code from the book doesn't work as expected, check the function's help page for any recent changes.

messages.subject: Species richness models
messages.body_plain:
Good morning all

I have a quick question regarding the Species richness models published by Dorazio and Royle.

These models entail including a matrix of 0's at the bottom of the detection/non-detection data set and then it uses MCMC to undertake the sampling. The 0's represent those species that one has not seen during the course of the study.

Assuming that one wants to include SPECIES SPECIFIC covariates (say body mass, ...) into the detection process, how would one do this for the unobserved species? Assuming here that we do not know the names of the unobserved species!!!

My initial idea was to consider imputation and simulate pseudo covariates that relates to the unobserved species and then use the MCMC algorithms as before. Given that these models actually take a long time to run, the imputation idea seems rather bad - unless it can be paralleled which it can.

Has anyone considered doing this???

Regards

messages.subject: Re: Species richness models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Allan,

at least for the "species-poor" taxa in well-studied countries/regions of the world (typlical examples birds, for instance, in Switzerland or the US), we know exactly the list of the species that could occur somewhere. So instead of data-augmenting 'blindly' one could take the full country list as a background and then use the known species size or mass or whatever covariate values.

If one does not have the luxury of this extra information, then I think one would have either avoid using such "individual" covariates or else estimate their values for the unobserved "individuals" (= species).

Best regards  ---- Marc

Good morning all

I have a quick question regarding the Species richness models published by Dorazio and Royle.

These models entail including a matrix of 0's at the bottom of the detection/non-detection data set and then it uses MCMC to undertake the sampling. The 0's represent those species that one has not seen during the course of the study.

Assuming that one wants to include SPECIES SPECIFIC covariates (say body mass, ...) into the detection process, how would one do this for the unobserved species? Assuming here that we do not know the names of the unobserved species!!!

My initial idea was to consider imputation and simulate pseudo covariates that relates to the unobserved species and then use the MCMC algorithms as before. Given that these models actually take a long time to run, the imputation idea seems rather bad - unless it can be paralleled which it can.

Has anyone considered doing this???

Regards

messages.subject: Re: Species richness models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Allan,

I'd like to build off of Marc's great response.

First, as a clarification, there is no requirement in using the community occupancy models of Dorazio and Royle (aka "Multi-species occupancy models") of adding in all-zero species (i.e., data augmentation). Many people who are interested in using these models are interested in alpha or beta diversity, in which case data augmentation has debatable added benefit. Data augmentation generally tells you how many species are in the community yet were not detected at *any* of your sample sites, which is to say, it gives you an estimate of true gamma diversity. Without data augmentation, you can still get at the number of "known" species that were not detected at a given site, yet which were detected at other sites. We tried to illustrate the differences between these two pools of "missing" species in Figure 2 of a paper we published a few years ago (Iknayan et al. 2014. TREE 29:97–106). So, if you don't actually care about gamma diversity, but are mostly interested in relative differences in alpha diversity, then you may not even need to do data augmentation.

Second, adding traits as hierarchical predictors of species-specific traits is a great idea. Luke Frishkoff recently published (Frishkoff et al. 2017. Ecology 98:198–210) a very nice framework for integrating traits and phylogeny into the hierarchical structure of these models that you may wish to investigate more (read the extensions section).

Cheers,
Morgan

--

University of Connecticut
